title: Constitutional Amendment to Keep the State Income Tax Rate from Being Raised Higher than 3.5%

context.text: Referred to the ballot by the General Assembly as Senate Bill 1080 (Session Law 2026-4), ratified May 21, 2026; primary sponsors are Sens. Michael Lee (R-New Hanover), Benton Sawrey and Lisa Barnes. The third-reading roll calls were 30-18 in the Senate and 73-46 in the House. Carolina Journal reported the amendment is part of the state budget framework agreement announced by Senate leader Phil Berger. Voters approved a 2018 amendment lowering the cap from 10% to 7%.

question.text: [ ] FOR [ ] AGAINST Constitutional amendment to keep the State income tax rate from being raised higher than three and one-half percent (3.5%).

summary.text: The amendment would amend Article V, Section 2(6) of the North Carolina Constitution to lower the maximum rate of tax on incomes from 7 percent to 3.5 percent. If approved it would take effect upon certification and apply to taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2027. Raising the rate above 3.5 percent would then require another constitutional amendment. WUNC reported that the current state budget already schedules the rate to fall from 3.99% to 3.49% in 2027; the amendment would make a cap permanent in the Constitution. The session law contains no fiscal estimate.

measure.yesMeans: Lowers the maximum state income tax rate allowed by the Constitution from 7% to 3.5%, so the rate could not be raised above 3.5% without another amendment.
measure.noMeans: Leaves the constitutional maximum income tax rate at 7%.

argumentsFor.text: Sen. Michael Lee (R-New Hanover) said in a statement to WECT: "Our tax reforms have produced more than a decade of strong revenue growth while letting people keep more of what they earn, and this amendment locks in that progress. I'm encouraging North Carolinians to vote yes in November. This is their decision to make, and it's a chance to put a real, lasting protection in the constitution for every taxpayer in the state."

argumentsAgainst.text: Gov. Josh Stein (D) called the amendment, at a May 27, 2026 press conference, "a con, a cynical shell game and a millionaire protection cap," and said: "We have to have a balanced budget every year when revenues are needed. You know who's going to have to pay? It's you. Regular people every time they go buy something through the sales tax."

The NC Budget & Tax Center said: "Income tax limits don't impact the total state and local taxes paid by North Carolinians. A limit on the income tax rate won't keep total state and local taxes low. In reality, states with income tax limits or no income tax tend to rely more on sales taxes, property taxes, and fees to fund the programs and services that are necessary to move our communities forward."

researchNotes: Ballot question text is taken verbatim from the question set out in the ratified session law, which is the text the State Board of Elections is directed to use on ballots. The North Carolina State Board of Elections' certified list could not be loaded (its pages list no ballot-question text); the three statewide amendments rest on the session laws and WUNC's September 22, 2026 explainer, which says voters will decide three proposed amendments, and the question wording is taken from the session laws. North Carolina has no citizen initiative and publishes no voter-pamphlet arguments; arguments are attributed quotes from news reports. A simple majority of votes cast on the question approves each amendment. Lee's and Stein's statements are as quoted in the cited reports; the NC Budget & Tax Center is an advocacy research group and is quoted as an organization's stated position.
